title: Cars Owned by Dictators: Almost Everything You’d Ever Want to Know

body_markdown:
At this year’s EyesOn Design car show, held annually at the home of Edsel and Eleanor Ford in Grosse Pointe Shores, Michigan, I spotted a 1973 Mercedes-Benz 600 “Pullman” six-door limousine from the collection of Samuel and Dena Lombardo. Also known as the Großer (“Grosser”) Mercedes, the 600 Pullman is a magnificent automobile that, in many ways, is still technically advanced even in 2026. While observing the limo, I thought to myself, “It’s a great car, but would you want to drive around in something associated with some of the worst people in history, like Idi Amin?”


The Ugandan dictator, known as “the Butcher of Uganda,” was so closely associated with Mercedes-Benzes that when Israel Defense Forces commandos raided Entebbe International Airport to liberate hijacked airliner passengers on July 4, 1976, they brought a black Mercedes (albeit a rather pedestrian 220D) to sneak past security checkpoints.


IDF


As I was photographing the big Benz, a fellow attendee told me that very car was made for Nicolae Ceaușescu. If that name doesn’t quite ring a bell, Ceaușescu was the communist dictator who ruled Romania with an iron fist for nearly 25 years. He’s[perhaps best known for his inability to read a room](https://youtu.be/t6pvMFfQF50?t=41) . Subsequently, while looking into this particular 600’s provenance, I discovered that it was delivered to a wealthy German family, not Ceaușescu. As of 2017, Ceaușescu’s six-door 600 was owned by French collector Olivier Delafon. Nonetheless, the passerby’s assertion confirmed the model’s popular association with evil with his assertion.


The confusion is understandable, as the Romanian tyrant was known for having more than one Mercedes. In addition to the cars used for state events, Ceaușescu also had a 1973 350SL that was fitted with a shortwave radio transmitter/receiver in the glove box, so the dictator could communicate with security forces.


When I pitched Ceaușescu’s car to my editor, he suggested that it would be a good time to update[our last look at dictators’ cars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/cars-of-the-real-dictators/) .


While the W100 series Mercedes-Benz 600 was owned by stratospheric celebrities like Elvis Presley, John Lennon, and George Harrison, along with great actors like Jack Nicholson and Elizabeth Taylor, the list of genuinely bad actors who also owned a 600 is a veritable rogues’ gallery of dictators and tyrants. Some of those dictators’ cars were limousines, including the six-door iteration like Ceaușescu’s. Since dictators love a parade, a few were open, landaulet cars. More than one dictator owned more than one Pullman. Some of the more notorious Mercedes-Benz 600 owners besides Idi and Nicolae have been Saddam Hussein (Iraq), Mao Zedong (China), Kim Il-Sung and Kim Jong-il (North Korea), Fidel Castro (Cuba), Josip Broz Tito (Yugoslavia), Ferdinand Marcos (Philippines), Pol Pot (Cambodia, see below), Leonid Brezhnev (USSR), Enver Hoxha (Albania), and Jean-Bédel Bokassa (Central African Republic).


The Benz, though, isn’t the only car favored by dictators. After all, if you essentially own a country, you’re likely to have more than one set of wheels, so some of the above-mentioned bad Benz guys will also appear in the list of dictators’ cars below.


## Rafael Trujillo


Rafael Trujillo pretty much ran the Dominican Republic for over 30 years, even when he wasn’t officially president. He is said to have favored Italian exotics, like Ferraris, but his last ride was a 1957 Chevy Bel-Air, in which he was ambushed and gunned down in 1961.


Universal History Archive/Getty Images


## Joseph Stalin


Joseph Stalin, who headed the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) from 1922 to 1953, liked Packards. Wayne Lensing’s Historic Attractions Museum near Rockford, Illinois, has the Soviet dictator’s armored 1937 Packard limousine on display along with a number of other cars that belonged to notorious tyrants. (The museum also has an extensive collection of American presidents’ limos and cars.) The Packard’s entire body is protected with steel armor plate. The bulletproof windows are three inches thick, and so heavy they require a hydraulic system to raise and lower them. Even the tires are bulletproof. Though it was mighty for the era, Packard’s 473-cubic-inch V-12 must have struggled to motivate the limo; with the modifications, it weighs in at 7.5 tons.


Stalin’s Packard


Ronnie Schreiber


Stalin liked Packards so much that he had a Soviet automobile manufacturer, ZiS, reverse-engineer Packard’s Super Eight into armored (ZiS-115) and non-armored (ZiS-110) versions. ZiS started out in 1916 as AMO (spelled out, the acronym translates as Moscow Automotive Society), making Fiat trucks under license. The works were renamed the First State Automobile Plant after the 1917 Russian Revolution. The facility underwent substantial renovation in the early 1930s, with the installation of conveyors for assembly-line production, and in 1931 it was renamed to ZiS (ЗИС), short for Zavod imeni Stalina, or “Factory Named After Stalin.” During de-Stalinization in the mid-1950s, it was renamed again, this time to ZiL, short for Zavod imeni Likhachyova (Factory Named After Likhachov) after longtime works director Ivan Likhachev.


Stalin’s ZiS-115


Wiki Commons


## Jean-Claude “Baby Doc” Duvalier


Jean-Claude “Baby Doc” Duvalier of Haiti inherited his position from his father, the infamous François “Papa Doc” Duvalier, who murdered tens of thousands of his own countrymen. Jean-Claude was literally made “President-For-Life” at the age of 19 in 1971 (hence the nickname, Baby Doc), ruling autocratically until he was deposed in 1986. The junior Duvalier was somewhat less authoritarian than his father, and more concerned with his own comfort and luxury. For example, Baby Doc liked Ferraris. During his rule, he drove a 365 GT 2+2 and a metallic green 400i. In exile on the French Riviera, he could be seen driving a red Testarossa.


He didn’t restrict himself to Ferraris, of course. Here, Jean-Claude “Baby Doc” Duvalier flees Haiti for exile on February 7, 1986, in the early morning hours, in a BMW.


Jean-Claude Francolon/Gamma-Rapho/Getty Images


## Fidel Castro


Fidel Castro may have hated the United States of America, but, like his fellow Cubans, he loved American cars, particularly Fords, Chevys, and Oldsmobiles in the 1940s and 1950s. During the revolution and afterward, he liked to be photographed driving Jeeps and their Soviet analogs.


Fidel Castro chauffeuring Saddam Hussein in a Russian jeep.


AFP/Getty Images


While he liked to be photographed in military vehicles, as president and dictator, Castro generally traveled in luxury. Following the revolution, after the U.S. embargoed Cuba, he switched from American domestics to European luxury brands, including his Mercedes-Benz 600 and a 500 SEL that’s in the Castro museum in Havana. However, his patron was the Soviet Union, so he also used a number of Soviet limos, including ZiLs. He was particularly associated, though, with another Russian car, the GAZ Chaika, later turning state Chaikas over to the state-run taxi fleet.


GAZ Chaika


Wiki Commons


## Vladimir Lenin


He ushered in the revolution of the proletariat, but as his automotive tastes indicated, Soviet Russian dictator Vladimir Lenin did not come from the working class. Communist ideology may have explicitly opposed bourgeois luxury, but as George Orwell taught us about revolutions, some animals end up more equal than others. Over the course of his seven-year rule, Lenin had the use of nine Rolls-Royce automobiles. He first grew to admire the robustness of the British luxury marque when he was in exile in Paris in 1910, after witnessing a Silver Ghost survive a serious collision relatively unscathed.


In the wake of the 1917 October Revolution, Lenin gained the use of the Rolls-Royces in the motorcade fleet of the deposed Tsar Nicholas, but Lenin’s best-known Rolls-Royce was purchased specifically for him. In 1922, one of Lenin’s emissaries purchased a Silver Ghost, which was converted into a half-track by French engineer Adolphe Kégresse. The tracked vehicle made it possible for Lenin to travel on the mostly undeveloped roads of the USSR, and through the snow, ice, and mud of harsh Russian winters. Naturally, the half-track Rolls became his primary vehicle for winter travel. It is currently on display at the Gorki-Leninskiye Museum near Moscow.


Wiki Commons


## Saddam Hussein


Saddam Hussein’s son Uday accumulated a substantial car collection, reportedly numbering in the hundreds. While the junior Hussein favored exotics, including a Lamborghini LM002 (which the U.S. Army later used for target practice), a Ferrari F40, and a pink Testarossa, his father’s tastes ran more toward traditional luxury cars. When American soldiers arrived at Hussein’s palace, they found about 60 collectible cars stored in two garages.


A Marine passes a 1932 Rolls-Royce Derby in Baghdad’s municipal basement on April 14, 2003.


Ramzi Haidar/AFP/Getty Images


The senior Hussein’s collection included a 1958 Rolls‑Royce Silver Cloud, the aforementioned Mercedes‑Benz 600 Pullman (an armored landaulet), a Cadillac Eldorado, a Bentley Mulsanne, a Packard convertible from the 1930s, a 1955 Chevrolet Bel Air, and an armored Cadillac Fleetwood.


Hussein also owned another Bentley,[a 1958 Bentley S1 Continental Drophead Coupe by Park Ward](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1958-bentley-s1-continental-3/) . That car had been delivered new to the former Crown Prince of the Hashemite Kingdom of Iraq in 1958. After the royal family was overthrown, a Baghdad businessman purchased the car and owned it for several years until Saddam Hussein decided to exercise his prerogative as a dictator and seized the Bentley for his personal use. After Hussein was overthrown, American authorities returned the car to its original owner. Many of the Husseins’ other cars have either been looted or destroyed.


The 1958 Bentley S1 Continental Drophead Coupe by Park Ward was bid to $1,735,000 on Bring a Trailer in ’25.


Bring a Trailer


## Muammar Gaddafi


Muammar Muhammad Abu Minyar al-Gaddafi was a Libyan military officer who deposed that country’s King Idris I in 1969 and ruled over that Mediterranean country with a revolutionary nationalistic fervor until he was deposed in a coup in 2011. As part of that nationalism, Gaddafi wanted Libya to produce its own automobile, which he supposedly designed himself. First introduced in September 1999, at the meeting of the Organization of African Unity, to celebrate the 30th anniversary of the revolution, the Saroukh el-Jamahiriya (“Missile of the People’s Mass Republic”) was claimed to be the safest car in the world. The five-passenger sedan had collapsible, rocket-shaped front and rear ends, airbags, and an “electronic defense system.” The Libyan Arab Domestic Investment Company (LADICO) produced the prototype and said that they would set up a factory to begin production within a month.


Georges Merillon/Gamma-Rapho/Getty Images


That never came to fruition, though in 2009, Col. Gaddafi introduced a second prototype, this time in white, and said it was to be developed to Gaddafi’s specifications at a cost of 2 million euros by Italian design firm Tesco TS SpA. There is no word on the fate of either Missile of the People’s Mass Republic following the 2011 coup. Gaddafi also had a custom, battery-powered Fiat 500 that, depending on the source, cost either $130,000 or $250,000 to build. Because of Libya’s intense heat, the Fiat EV has an air conditioner powered by a combustion engine.


AFP/Getty Images


## Adolf Hitler


No list of dictators and their cars would be complete without the failed Austrian painter with the funny mustache who ruled over Germany (and eventually much of Europe) from 1933 to 1945. Much as it may bother us enthusiasts, Adolf Hitler was a bit of a car guy. His[National Socialist government directly funded](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/3082312-hitler-s-motor-racing-battles) the Mercedes-Benz and[Auto Union “Silver Arrow”](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/in-the-moment-a-dictator-and-a-v-16/) grand prix racing efforts and built the Autobahn network of high-speed intercity highways. Hitler famously backed Ferdinand Porsche’s “People’s Car” project that produced the Volkswagen, even supplying Dr. Porsche with concept sketches.


Note the initials, A.H.


However, Adolf Hitler had a special attachment to big Benzes, saying that he would “not tolerate a car manufactured by another company.” After the assassination in 1942 of Reinhard Heydrich, one of the architects of the Holocaust, Hitler commissioned Mercedes-Benz to produce about 20 bulletproof, closed-bodied[540K “Aktion Panzer”](https://www.caranddriver.com/features/a65614574/mercedes-benz-540k-aktion-panzer-car-barn-find/) models for his inner circle that were protected with thick glass and steel armor plate. Mercedes-Benz also produced a number of armored Großer (“Grosser”) Mercedes 770Ks for the use of Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis officials.


Hitler riding in the Großer Mercedes-Benz 770K in Berlin.


Archive Photos/Getty Images


Adolf even had his own G-Wagon. Mercedes-Benz produced 57 W31 Type G4 “Cross Country” three-axle six-wheelers for the regime that the automaker stated were intended for “Staat, Partei, und Wehrmacht,” or Government, Party, and armed forces use. Though intended to be used as a field or staff car, the G4 was most infamously used as a parade car for Hitler himself. Wayne Lensing’s collection includes one of the three surviving G4s.


Ronnie Schreiber


## Benito Mussolini


Italian dictator Benito Mussolini’s favorite cars were Alfa Romeos, and he even wrote a fan letter to Nicola Romeo praising one of the Alfas that he owned. During his rule over Italy, he owned a minimum of two 6C 2300 Spiders, a 1500 sedan, a 1500 convertible, and[four 1750s](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/nut-and-bolt-restoration-of-mussolinis-1930-alfa-romeo/) . He even hired racer Ercole Boratto, who drove Mussolini’s own 6C 2300 in the 1936 Mille Miglia, as his personal chauffeur. It was in an Alfa Romeo 6C Sport Berlinetta that Mussolini and his mistress, Clara Petacci, tried to flee Italy after his regime fell.


Mussolini-owned Alfa Romeo 6C 1750 SS


Ashley Border/Lightflow/Thornley Kelham


While Mussolini preferred to drive Alfa Romeos, when he was driven in state events, he rode in the back of a 1939 Lancia Astura, purchased by the Italian Ministry of the Interior specifically for Mussolini’s use.


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


## Hirohito


Emperor Michi Hirohito was the 124th Emperor of Japan. The longest surviving and longest reigning emperor of Japan, as well as the last monarch on earth to be an absolute ruler with the hereditary title of Emperor, he ruled over Japan when it attacked the United States’ naval base at Pearl Harbor, bringing the U.S. into the Second World War in December 1941.


There’s no record of whether the emperor was ever behind the wheel himself, but like his ally Hitler, Hirohito had a Mercedes-Benz 770 model. In the case of His Royal Highness, it was a 1935 Grand Pullman limousine, one of only 117 that Mercedes-Benz produced. Perhaps surprisingly for a monarch whose subjects considered him to be a living god, the limo’s roof and doors were armored for his protection.


Wiki Commons


Hirohito was also chauffeured in a 1935 Packard Model 1202 eight-cylinder limousine, currently in the Lensing collection.


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


## Kim Jong Un


Kim Il Sung founded the communist Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (also known as North Korea) in 1948. Kim apparently liked Mercedes-Benz automobiles, and he passed that affection, as well as his position, on to his son, Kim Jong Il. North Korea’s second dictator liked the brand so much that he reportedly spent 25% of an $80 million international aid package on Mercedes-Benz cars he gave to the country’s rocket scientists as a reward for a successful ballistic missile test. He also is said to have distributed 160 Benz sedans to regime loyalists in 2010. His personal cars were Maybachs and a S600 Pullman Guard armored limo, though he was carried to his grave on top of a Lincoln Continental limousine.


Kim Jong Il was succeeded by his son Kim Jong Un, whose ability to acquire high-end Mercedes-Benz products despite international sanctions has attracted the attention of the United Nations. In addition to S600 Pullman Guards in both closed and landaulet parade versions, the youngest Kim also has an Aurus armored limo that was gifted to him by Russian dictator Vladimir Putin.


Pyeongyang Press Corps/Pool/Getty Images


Pyeongyang Press Corps/Pool/Getty Images


Gavriil Grigorov/Pool/Getty Images


Kyodo News/AFP/Getty Images


## Pol Pot


Pol Pot, the leader of the communist Cambodian Khmer Rouge revolutionaries, oversaw one of the worst genocides of the 20th century, killing approximately 2 million of his fellow countrymen and women between 1976 and 1979, or about a quarter of the country’s entire population. Some people were literally buried alive after digging their own graves to save bullets.


Pol Pot on the left in front of the Mercedes.


Frederic Amat/Sygma/Getty Images


Like many other dictators, Pol Pot liked Mercedes-Benzes. Sources on the 600 Pullman say that he had one of those, as well as a short-wheelbase W115, which appears to be the car in the photo above. However, the only photos that I could find of a Mercedes-Benz limousine associated with Pol Pot appear to be of a diesel-powered W115-based 220D Lang Pullman, not the W100-based Großer 600.


Tang Chhin Sothy/AFP/Getty Images


## Juan Perón


In 1943, Juan Perón was one of a group of Argentinian military officers who staged a coup against the civilian government. He rose through ministerial ranks to become vice president by 1944 and was elected president of the South American country in 1946. A populist authoritarian, he was supported by the rank-and-file military and by the country’s laborers, known as *descamisados* or “shirtless ones.” He severely restricted constitutional liberties and pushed through legislation to allow him to repeatedly run for reelection. Perón’s political partner was his wife, María Eva Duarte de Perón, known as Evita to the Argentinian masses, who are said to have adored her. A glamorous actress before their marriage, she supported Perón’s administration and policies with frequent public appearances. Evita died of cancer in 1952, and Juan Perón was deposed and driven into exile by a coup in 1955.


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


The Peróns used an armored 1950 Rolls-Royce Silver Wraith limousine as a state car. While the chauffeur of the town car was completely exposed, the passenger compartment had armor plating in the doors, body panels, and floor, plus one-inch-thick glass in all the windows, including the partition between the cabin and the driver.


For his personal cars, Perón favored Ferraris, his favorite being a[1952 212 Inter Coupe by Ghia](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/az18/lots/r196-1952-ferrari-212-inter-coupe-by-ghia/) . Powered by a 170-hp V-12 engine, the car was nominally one of 73 Inter Coupes made but was actually a one-off show car. Ghia clothed it in custom bodywork influenced by concepts the Italian coachbuilder was building at the behest of Virgil Exner, Sr., for Chrysler in that era. Perón’s car was given a particularly luxurious interior and was debuted at the 1952 Paris Motor Show, where Perón first saw it. To avoid the steep Argentine import taxes on new luxury cars, the president arranged for the Ferrari to be returned to Maranello, where it could be registered for road use and then imported to Argentina as a used car.


Bring a Trailer last auctioned off Perón’s 212 again for[$950,000 in 2019](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1952-ferrari-212/) .


Bring a Trailer


A car enthusiast, Perón had a collection of luxury and sporting automobiles described as “immense,” including, as mentioned, several Ferraris as well as a few Packards. A racing fan, he helped finance the career of the country’s rising star,[Juan Manuel Fangio](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/in-the-moment-just-keep-swimming/) , supporting Fangio and José Froilán González’s Gordini at Le Mans in 1950, and backing Fangio’s Formula 1 efforts, including having a F1 circuit built in Buenos Aires, which Perón named after himself. Perón even created a state-financed native Argentine automobile called the Justicialista, named after the Peronist political party.


Juan Perón with the Justicialista prototype at the Buenos Aires autodrome.


Wiki Commons


The production Justicialista had a front-wheel-drive layout powered by a two-stroke, two-cylinder engine based on a DKW design, and a steel body. Apparently, fewer than 200 were made from 1954 to 1955, when Perón was driven from power.


Production Justicialista


Wiki Commons


## Leonid Brezhnev


Leonid Brezhnev was the General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1964 to 1982, from the height of the Cold War through the end of the détente era with the United States. Brezhnev was a bit of a car enthusiast. In addition to the long-wheelbase ZiL-114 that was his official state car, Brezhnev ordered a ZiL-117, a short-wheelbase version, which he drove himself as a personal car. After a 1969 assassination attempt on Brezhnev, the ZiL factory developed the ZiL-4105 to be used by the General Secretary and other Kremlin leaders. It was said to be the most heavily armored passenger car in the world at the time.


ZiL-4105


Flickr


Knowing Brezhnev’s fondness for automobiles, a number of world leaders gave him cars, a strategy that some called Town Car Diplomacy. German chancellor Willy Brandt reportedly gave Brezhnev two Mercedes-Benzes: a W100-based six-door 600 Pullman, on the occasion of a treaty signing in Moscow in 1970; and a 450 SLC coupe, when Brezhnev made a state visit to Bonn, the German capital. According to many accounts, Brezhnev got behind the wheel of the SLC for a test drive up the winding road to the guest house and proceeded to wreck the car. Sources disagree as to whether it was repaired or just replaced.


Leonid Brezhnev’s 450 SLC


platesmania.com/slavchick_


At a 1973 summit at Camp David outside of Washington, D.C., President Richard Nixon gave the Soviet leader a blue Lincoln Continental with a vinyl roof, giving pause to Secret Service agents when Brezhnev fired it up and drove away—with Nixon in the passenger seat.


Public Domain


Brezhnev also had a V-8-powered Nissan President that was a gift from Hirohide Ishida, a former Japanese government minister. Today it is assumed that Ishida was a KGB asset and that the “gift” was arranged and funded by that Soviet security agency. Reportedly, Brezhnev chauffeured both President Nixon and U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger around Moscow in the suitably named vehicle.


Brezhnev’s Nissan President


Wojtek Laski/Getty Images


## Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue


Technically, Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue was not a dictator; he was only Vice President of Equatorial Guinea, though he got that position from his father, President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, who has ruled since 1979. That said, any time a “president” serves for over four decades, the appellation “dictator” likely applies to the family business.


Known for his lavish lifestyle, the junior Teodora was accused of numerous crimes, including embezzlement and corruption. While the country is oil-rich, most of the population lives in poverty, in stark contrast to Obiang Mangue’s automotive tastes. Many of the rulers on this list favored luxury cars, and Obiang Mangue indeed had his share of Bentleys, Rolls-Royces, Maybachs, and lesser Ferraris and Lambos. However, he stands out in this crowd for his collection of exotic, high-performance supercars, which he kept in Switzerland for when he visited Europe.


As part of broader investigations by the Swiss and French authorities into his corruption and misappropriation of public funds, his exotics were seized by Swiss officials and[auctioned off by Bonhams in 2019](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/supercar-collection-seized-headed-public-auction/) , with proceeds benefiting social programs in Equatorial Guinea. Those seized cars included a Lamborghini Veneno Roadster (one of just nine that were made), a Koenigsegg One:1, a Ferrari Enzo, a Ferrari LaFerrari, a McLaren P1, and an Aston Martin One-77. That group doesn’t include the Ferrari 599 GTO, Maserati MC12, Porsche Carrera GT, and assorted Bugattis that were previously seized and auctioned off.


Lamborghini Veneno Roadster


Wiki Commons


## Mao Zedong


Hongqi CA770


Wiki Commons


Mao Zedong ruled China as the chairman of the Chinese Communist Party from the revolution of 1949 until his death in 1976. It’s estimated that his regime was responsible for the deaths of over 40 million Chinese people during the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. His official state car was the Hongqi CA770, which was powered by a 5.6-liter V-8 that is rumored to have been copied from a Chrysler Imperial. As mentioned above, Chairman Mao was also a member of the 600 Pullman club.


## Nicolae Ceaușescu


Though a 600 Pullman Mercedes inspired this article, and Nicolae Ceaușescu did own one, I would be remiss if I did not acknowledge the fully loaded 1974 Buick Electra given to him by President Nixon (in another display of Town Car Diplomacy).


A Buick Electra similar to Ceaușescu’s.


Wiki Commons


## Josip Broz Tito


Josip Broz Tito was indeed a dictator over what was then Yugoslavia, but the country was a bit more open and more prosperous than most Soviet Bloc countries.[Tito was a member of the 600 Pullman club](https://www.salonpriveconcours.com/news/1970-mercedes-benz-600-pullman-presidential-long-top-landaulet/) when it came to parades and state events, but among his personal cars, his favorite was said to be a 1948 Packard Victoria convertible.


Keystone/Hulton Archive/Getty Images


## Vladimir Putin


Mikhail Svetlov/Getty Imagess


Vladimir Putin has essentially governed Russia since 1999, making him one of the world’s longest-reigning national leaders. His current official ride is an Aurus Senat limousine made by the Scientific Automotive Engines Institute, whose acronym works out to NAMI in Latin characters. NAMI has been around since 1920 and made the USSR’s first automobile. The Senat is said to have retro styling based on the 1945 ZiS-110, one of Stalin’s limos, but it has some clear influence from the modern-day Rolls-Royce Phantom and the American president’s “Beast.” The Senat’s hybrid powertrain is rated at an impressive 598 horsepower. The Russians claim that not only is Putin’s limo bulletproof and bomb-proof, but its passengers can also survive the vehicle being fully submerged in water. There’s no word, however, on whether it has underwater propulsion like James Bond’s Lotus.


Wiki Commons


## Tsar Nicholas II


Besides Putin, Lenin, and Stalin, another absolute ruler over Russia was Tsar Nicholas II, the last emperor of Russia, who reigned from 1894 until the Russian Revolution of 1917. His aide-de-camp, Prince Vladimir Nikolayevich Orlov, was an early motoring enthusiast who introduced the tsar to automobiles, driving the monarch in Orlov’s French-made Delaunay-Belleville. In the fall of 1905, Nicholas told Orlov to buy him “two or three cars,” leaving the choice to the prince’s discretion. Orlov chose a four-cylinder Delaunay-Belleville 40CV to be Russia’s first royal automobile.


Tsar Nicholas II (on horse) with his first automobile, the Delaunay-Belleville 40CV.


Public Domain


The tsar was so impressed he had Orlov order the more powerful six-cylinder 70CV model with a limousine body from the French automaker in 1909. Though it is hardly known today, the Delaunay Belleville 70CV was one of the most sophisticated early automobiles, with a self-starting system that pneumatically got the pistons reciprocating before you turned on the fuel and ignition. The pneumatic system also operated an on-board jacking system and provided compressed air to inflate tires. French coachbuilder Cologner & Fils was responsible for kitting out the interior with rosewood, a glass roof, and a sound-deadening double floor. The roof was even raised so the tsar, who stood five feet, six inches, could stand inside the passenger compartment.


Circa 1913: Emperor Nicholas II arriving in his Delaunay Belleville 70CV at the Fourth
International Automobile Exhibition, held at the Mikhailovsky Manege, St. Petersburg.


Public Domain


## Nikita Khrushchev


Nikita Khrushchev was First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from the death of Stalin in 1953 until the Politburo replaced him in 1964 following the Cuban Missile Crisis. Like other Soviet leaders, he used limousines and state cars made by ZiL, including the ZiL-111. ****


Besides Zavod imeni Likhachyova (ZiL), there was another Soviet automotive effort named after an important political figure: Zavod imeni Molotova, or ZiM, after famous cocktail mixologist Gen. Vyacheslav Molotov. Located in Nizhny Novgorod, the plant started out with Ford Motor Company’s assistance in 1932 as the Nizhny Novgorod Automobile Factory, originally assembling knock-down kits of the Model A car and Model AA trucks. A year later, the city was renamed to honor Russian author Maxim Gorky, and the plant’s name was changed to Gorky Automobile Zavod (Gorky Automobile Plant), or GAZ.


After Stalin’s death, Molotov fell out of favor with Politburo bosses, so the company name reverted to GAZ, and the cars rebranded accordingly. While it’s not technically a dictator’s car, the GAZ-12 ZIM seven-passenger pullman below was a gift from Comrade Khrushchev to the prime minister of Norway in 1950.


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


## Robert Mugabe


Robert Mugabe was prime minister of Zimbabwe from 1980 to 1987, and president from 1987 to 2017. Corrupt, authoritarian, and openly racist, Mugabe was an anti-imperialist who didn’t let that stance stop him from enjoying luxury. Only eighteen Rolls-Royce Phantom IVs were ever made, exclusively for heads of state and royalty. When Mugabe got his vintage Phantom landaulet, some critics claimed its value exceeded Zimbabwe’s GDP at the time. For events less ceremonial, Mugabe was chauffeured in a W140-series Mercedes-Benz 600 Pullman now on display in the country’s National Historical Institute.


STR/AFP/Getty Images


The Mugabe family does like their Rollers. Robert’s widow, Grace Mugabe, and her son Russell Goreraza have a collection of modern BMW-era Rolls-Royces including Ghosts and Wraiths.


Mugabe’s Mercedes-Benz S600 Pullman presidential limousine on display.


Wiki Commons


## Jean‑Bédel Bokassa


While the imperial house of Japan is the only remaining hereditary dynasty with the title “Emperor,” that doesn’t mean that there haven’t been any self-proclaimed emperors in the world since Hirohito. Jean‑Bédel Bokassa was president of the Central African Republic from 1966 to 1976, after which he declared himself to be Emperor Bokassa I of the Central African Empire from 1976 to 1979.


Bokassa’s rule was notorious for severe human rights abuses, economic mismanagement, corruption, and he was even accused of engaging in cannibalism. He was deposed by French troops in 1979. In 1977, he was crowned emperor in an elaborate ceremony, modeled on that of Napoleon, that cost a reported $22 million, the equivalent of about a quarter of the impoverished country’s annual budget.


Bokassa in his Mercedes-Benz 600 Landaulet with French president Valéry Giscard d’Estaing.


William Karel/Gamma-Rapho/Getty Images


Bokassa ordered approximately 60 brand-new Mercedes-Benz vehicles for the coronation motorcade (he had two 600 Pullman limos) that racked up $300,000 in shipping charges alone. Bokassa originally planned to ride to the ceremony with his wife in an[antique carriage similar to that of Napoleon, drawn by eight white horses imported from Europe for the event](https://artsandculture.google.com/asset/royal-carriages-mohamed-amin/XgF_65jADb_hbw) . However, the closed carriage proved to be too hot in the 95-degree weather, so the imperial couple switched to one of the air-conditioned Benzes for most of the procession until switching back to the ceremonial carriage a few hundred yards from the destination.


## Bonus: Studebaker Dictator


I suppose it would be appropriate, after reviewing all of these dictators’ cars, to close with a Dictator car. In 1927, Studebaker thought it was a good idea to rename their entry-level car, the Standard, to the Dictator, to better match their upmarket Commander and President models. The tagline was: “The car that dictates the standard.”


Studebaker


It was a curious choice, as Alfa Romeo fan Benito Mussolini had already been in power in Italy for four years by 1927, and Studebaker must have known the name presented some issues, as the car was branded “Director” in Europe. Even more curiously, after the Dictator model was dropped in 1933 for financial reasons due to the deepening Great Depression, it returned for the 1934 through ’37 model years. For 1938, it was renamed yet again, this time as “Commander.” I suppose that by then Hitler, Stalin, and Mussolini had given “Dictator” a bad smell.
